stories.headline: Federal officials identify 400 noncitizens registered to vote in Washington state: 'Tip of the iceberg'
stories.note: Hundreds of noncitizens on a blue state's rolls backs up the GOP's push for election integrity.
body: The Justice Department said Monday that federal investigators have found more than 400 noncitizens registered to vote in Washington state, and that many of them have voted in more than one election. Many of those flagged are green card holders living in the country legally.

Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd of the Western District of Washington said the list came from comparing immigration benefit records against voting records. By his office's count, the group cast roughly 1,500 ballots in all, with some people voting as many as 27 times and the earliest case going back to around 1984.

Floyd said the true number is likely much higher because the review only covered people who applied for certain benefits. "This is only the tip of the iceberg," he said, estimating the total could run into the thousands. He added that he hasn't checked whether any of them voted in the current midterms so as not to interfere with the election.

Officials said some green card holders were signed up without realizing it through the state's Motor Voter program at the Department of Licensing. The state's own website says automatic registration only applies to people who show proof of citizenship. The DOJ has asked Washington to set aside ballots from the identified voters until their citizenship can be confirmed, and separately DHS said dozens of noncitizens have been arrested nationwide in a voter fraud crackdown.

Why it matters: Hard numbers on noncitizen voting in a deep-blue state strengthen the Republican case for proof-of-citizenship rules and voter-roll cleanups, and put Democratic-run election systems on the defensive just days before the midterms.

stories.headline: DSA-affiliated Senate nominee sparks bipartisan uproar with comments on communist dictatorship
stories.note: A Democratic Senate nominee drawing fire from both parties over communism hands Republicans a gift a week before Election Day.
body: Florida's Democratic Senate nominee, state Rep. Angie Nixon, is under fire from both parties over how she answered a CBS News question about whether Cuba is a dictatorship. Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America earlier this year, said that is what people have told her but that she has never been to Cuba.

Nixon accused CBS of misrepresenting her, saying she had made clear she believes the Cubans who described it as a dictatorship. CBS deleted its first post about the exchange and reposted the clip with an editor's note saying the earlier version didn't accurately portray her answer.

The substance of her answer still drew pushback from fellow Democrats. Phil Ehr, the party's nominee in Florida's 28th District, said Cuban Americans he met at early voting sites were frightened, and said he would not defend her remarks. Elliott Rodriguez, the nominee in the 27th District, said Cuba being a dictatorship is a fact, not an opinion.

Republicans piled on. Sen. Rick Scott compared it to Democrats who can't define what a woman is, and Rep. Byron Donalds called it "the craziest thing I've ever heard." In an August interview Nixon had distanced herself from DSA's praise of Fidel Castro.

Why it matters: In a state shaped by Cuban exiles, a Democratic Senate nominee hedging on communist Cuba, and getting rebuked by her own party's House candidates, is a gift to Sen. Ashley Moody and Florida Republicans heading into Nov. 3.

stories.headline: 175 Democrats demand Trump admin stop Ilhan Omar investigation, warn it could hurt her re-election bid
stories.note: Most of the Democratic caucus going to bat for Omar ties the whole party to her legal troubles.
body: Led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, 175 House Democrats signed a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding they halt the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

Federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home on Oct. 12 under a court-approved warrant, taking phones and notebooks. Investigators are looking at whether Omar or her father misstated her birth year on immigration paperwork. If she was 18 or older when her father became a citizen, as officials now suspect, she would have needed to apply on her own.

The Democrats called the probe a politically driven attack and said acting this close to the election breaks long-standing DOJ practice. They wrote that news of the search could affect how voters in Minnesota's 5th District cast their ballots and told the officials they had "already disgraced the offices you hold."
Omar has called the investigation a political hit job. Republicans see it differently, and House Majority Whip Tom Emmer has said she should be jailed and deported if the accusations are proven.
Why it matters: With most of the House Democratic caucus formally standing behind Omar, Republicans can tie the broader party to her legal troubles in the final week of the campaign.

stories.headline: Watchdog accuses DSA candidate of blurring charity, business and campaign: 'What happened to all that money?'
stories.note: Money questions around a socialist Democratic candidate give Republicans another line of attack.
body: The National Legal and Policy Center, a conservative watchdog, filed a complaint Monday against Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon, asking the FEC, IRS, the U.S. Attorney's Office and Florida's attorney general to look into her now-defunct nonprofit, the Moxie Group.

The group points to the charity's 2024 filing, where about $210,000 in spending was listed only as "other" without the itemization the form calls for. It also notes the nonprofit's license for a Jacksonville bookstore and coffee shop, Café Resistance, was moved to Nixon's for-profit company of the same name.

The complaint also questions whether the charity kept soliciting tax-deductible donations after its board voted to disband in December 2025, since it didn't file dissolution papers until Oct. 1 of this year. And it argues the café acting as a campaign hub, including a phone bank listed on Nixon's campaign site, could break campaign finance rules if it wasn't paid for.

Nixon's campaign disputes all of it. It says she stepped down from the nonprofit in December 2025, played no role in its later decisions, has paid nothing to the café because it only used the parking lot, and doesn't own the building. Fox said it isn't aware of any donations made to the charity after it disbanded.
Why it matters: On top of the Cuba controversy, money questions give Sen. Ashley Moody another line of attack against a socialist-backed opponent with a week to go.

stories.headline: Haitian illegal immigrant charged in Walmart killing entered US via Biden parole program: DHS
stories.note: Linking a killing to Biden's parole program keeps the border failures of the last administration front and center.
body: A 23-year-old Haitian man charged with murdering a Walmart employee outside a Pennsylvania store came into the country through the Biden administration's CHNV parole program, DHS sources told Fox News.

Destino Jean-Louis is accused of shooting 45-year-old Latosha Ann Cooper on Oct. 21 outside the Walmart in Cheltenham Township, Montgomery County. According to DHS sources, he flew into Fort Lauderdale under the parole program in November 2023, and his legal status was revoked in June 2025. ICE arrested him in Philadelphia on Oct. 23 and handed him to local authorities on Oct. 26.

Local reports citing court documents say the two met working at the store and married after Cooper offered to help him get a green card. After his application was denied in July, she pulled out and cut off contact. Investigators allege he asked co-workers for her schedule, waited masked near the store, and shot her as she left her night shift; cellphone records allegedly put him there that night and on earlier nights.

He faces charges including first- and third-degree murder and firearms counts, is being held without bail, and has denied being at the store. DHS said that under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, "if you break the law, you will face the consequences."
Why it matters: The case puts a face on Republican criticism of Biden-era mass parole programs and reinforces the GOP's message on border security and enforcement.

stories.headline: Rep Tom Tiffany claims Kamala Harris' visit signals weakness in David Crowley's Wisconsin campaign
stories.note: Tiffany frames Harris's late rescue trip as a sign Democrats are worried in Wisconsin.
body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned in Milwaukee on Monday for Democratic governor candidate David Crowley, just eight days before Election Day. His Republican opponent, Rep. Tom Tiffany, says the visit shows Crowley is in trouble.
"David Crowley has not excited the base," Tiffany told Fox News Digital, arguing Democrats brought Harris in because they are struggling to get their voters to turn out.

Tiffany also repeated the charge that party leaders, including Gov. Tony Evers, handpicked Crowley as a centrist over progressives like state Rep. Francesca Hong, whom he narrowly beat in the primary. He compared it to how Harris herself became the nominee, and hit Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, as someone who raises taxes every year.

Crowley's campaign fired back, saying he is traveling the state with a plan to lower costs, that he balanced the budget and cut the property tax rate every year, and that Tiffany sold out Wisconsinites to give billionaires tax breaks.
Why it matters: Wisconsin's governorship is a top battleground, and Republicans want voters to read a late Harris rescue trip as a sign of Democratic weakness rather than strength.

stories.headline: Inside Melania Trump's secret diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire deal
stories.note: A behind-the-scenes look at the first lady's role burnishes the Trump team's peacemaking record.
body: First lady Melania Trump quietly brokered a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, to allow food, water, medicine and doctors in and give residents a safe way out, Fox News Digital reported in an exclusive.

According to her senior adviser Marc Beckman, both Kyiv and Moscow formally named her their "exclusive intermediary," with Putin and Zelenskyy involved in the talks. She had already helped reunite 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families, which built the trust needed for this deal.

Russian and Ukrainian human rights officials signed the agreement in Belarus on Oct. 23 after an overnight session the first lady joined by video. The plan, worked out down to the hour, covers which equipment can enter, how civilians are evacuated, and even refrigerated trucks for recovering bodies. The ceasefire began early Tuesday and was widened to give aid convoys safe passage across the Kherson region; Russia's top general confirmed it.

Oleshky has shrunk from about 24,000 people to around 2,000, many elderly, and sits right on the front line. The deal is limited to this humanitarian operation and doesn't stop fighting elsewhere, but it calls for monthly aid and repatriation efforts across Kherson coordinated with the first lady.
Why it matters: A concrete pause in fighting, achieved by the first lady with a tiny team, adds to the Trump administration's case that it can deliver results on ending the war.
